opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about it in a few layers. The first thing is that every enterprise's tools are a little bit idiosyncratic. You have internal APIs, internal databases, maybe some custom schemas that nobody outside the company has ever seen. So a general-purpose model, even a really strong one, doesn't come in knowing how those tools behave, what the failure modes are, or what "good" looks like in that environment.

So the starting point is really about the data. You want to collect trajectories of the model actually interacting with those tools: what call it made, what came back, how it recovered when something broke. In a lot of cases you don't have that data lying around, so you end up generating it synthetically. You can use a stronger model as a teacher, or you can set up an environment where the model explores and you filter for successful runs. Data curation is where most of the leverage is, honestly, more than the choice of architecture or even the exact training recipe.

Then there's the training itself. Supervised fine-tuning on good trajectories gets you surprisingly far, especially for teaching the format and the basic patterns of tool use. But where things get really interesting is reinforcement learning, because tool use has a nice property: you can often verify outcomes. Did the query return the right rows? Did the ticket get filed correctly? If you can build a reward around that, you can let the model improve beyond what your demonstrations showed it.

And the reason to do this with an open-source model, rather than just calling a frontier API, is control. Enterprises care about where their data goes, they care about cost at scale, and they care about latency. A smaller open model that's been specialized for their specific tool set can often match or beat a much bigger general model on that narrow distribution, while being cheaper to run and deployable inside their own infrastructure.

The last piece I'd emphasize is evaluation. People tend to underinvest there. You need a realistic eval set that reflects the actual tasks people in the company do, not just generic benchmarks. Otherwise you don't really know if your fine-tuning helped, or if you've just overfit to your synthetic data. So build the eval early, iterate on data, and treat the whole thing as a loop rather than a one-shot training run.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes supervised fine-tuning on tool-use trajectories and reinforcement learning with outcome-based rewards as complementary training methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the hard part isn't really the model, it's the environment. When people say "train a model to use our tools," what they usually have in their head is: take an open model, give it a bunch of examples of correct tool calls, fine-tune it, done. And that works a little bit, but it's brittle, because tool use is fundamentally a multi-step, interactive problem. The model calls a tool, it gets back some response it's never seen before, it has to decide what to do next. You can't capture that with a static dataset of input-output pairs. You have to actually let the model interact with the tools.

So the first thing we do is build an environment that mirrors the enterprise's actual stack. That means the real APIs, or faithful simulations of them, with the same schemas, the same error messages, the same weird edge cases. If your CRM returns a 429 when you hit it too fast, the training environment should do that too. A lot of the value is just in that fidelity. If the model only ever sees happy-path tool responses during training, it falls apart the first time something goes sideways in production.

The second piece is the reward signal. In an enterprise setting you often have something close to ground truth: did the ticket get resolved, did the record get updated correctly, did the SQL query return the right rows. Those are verifiable outcomes, and that's what makes reinforcement learning viable here. You're not relying on a vague preference model saying "this looks good." You can actually check whether the task got done. So we lean heavily on RL with those verifiable rewards, and we use supervised fine-tuning mostly as a warm start so the model knows the basic format and vocabulary of the tools before it starts exploring.

The third thing, and this is where open source really matters, is that the tools and the data are the moat for the enterprise. They're not going to send their internal API traces to a closed-model provider, and even if they would, they'd be stuck with whatever that provider's tool-calling format and behavior happens to be. With an open model you can keep everything in your own infrastructure, you can shape the model's behavior around your specific tools, and you end up with something that's often smaller and cheaper than a frontier model but better at your particular tasks, because it's actually practiced on them.

And then the last thing I'd say is you have to think about it as a continuous process rather than a one-shot training run. Enterprise tools change constantly. Someone adds a field, deprecates an endpoint, changes a permission model. So the environment and the eval suite have to be living artifacts, and you want a loop where production traces, with appropriate filtering, flow back into training. The model should be getting better as the tools evolve, not drifting out of date.

r001.rationale: It says they rely on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and use supervised fine-tuning as a warm start for tool formats and vocabulary.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to separate knowing about the enterprise from knowing how to use its tools. You don’t necessarily want to put all of the enterprise’s knowledge into the model’s weights. That information changes, and access to it depends on who’s asking. What you want the model to learn is how to get the right information through the tools that are available to it.

So you might start with an open-source model and train it on examples of tool use: given a request and a set of tool descriptions, which tool should it call, what arguments should it provide, and how should it interpret the result? And sometimes the right behavior is to ask a clarifying question rather than call a tool.

The interesting challenge is generalization. If you train it on a fixed set of APIs, does it just memorize those APIs, or can it use a new tool from its description? I’d want to evaluate that explicitly, with tools it hasn’t seen during training, and measure whether it actually completes the task—not just whether it generates a valid function call.

And then permissions need to be enforced by the system executing those calls. The model can propose an action, but the enterprise’s access controls should determine whether that action is allowed.

r001.rationale: The response describes training on tool-use examples, but it does not identify reinforcement learning or a combination of reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as teaching the model how to interact with tools, and then giving it the enterprise-specific context it needs at runtime. You don’t necessarily want to retrain the model every time somebody adds an API or changes a tool.

For example, you might give the model a question and a set of tool descriptions. It has to learn which tool is relevant, what arguments to provide, and how to use the result. Sometimes that means calling another tool; sometimes it means asking the user for information that’s missing.

With an open-source model, you can fine-tune on examples of those interactions. But I’d want to evaluate whether it can use tools it hasn’t seen during training. Has it learned to read a tool description and reason about how to use it, or has it just memorized particular calls? That ability to generalize is what makes the approach useful across different enterprises.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fine-tuning on tool-use examples, but does not identify reinforcement learning as part of the training approach.
